title: I Have $900k in My IRA. Here’s the Yearly Roth Conversion That Dodges the Next Tax Bracket.
summary: Retirees with large traditional IRAs can plan Roth conversions around tax brackets to keep future RMDs from raising their taxes.
body_markdown:
Having a large balance in a traditional IRA can lead to required[minimum distributions (RMDs)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/calculate-rmd) that push you into a higher tax bracket later in retirement. To reduce that risk, some retirement savers[convert part of their IRA to a Roth](https://smartasset.com/retirement/partial-roth-conversion) at strategic times, which can lower future RMDs and help manage taxable income. Here’s an example that shows how annual conversions on a $900,000 IRA could affect your taxes over time.


## How to Calculate a Roth Conversion That Stays in Your Tax Bracket


[RMDs begin at 73](https://smartasset.com/retirement/when-does-the-rmd-age-go-up-to-75-years-old) for people born between 1951 and 1959, and 75 for those born in 1960 or later. To calculate your RMD, divide your IRA balance from December 31 of the previous year by a life expectancy factor from the[IRS’s Uniform Lifetime Table](https://smartasset.com/retirement/rmd-table) .


The factor is based on your age. At 75, for example, the factor is 24.6, and with a $900,000 IRA, your RMD would be $36,585 ($900,000 ÷ 24.6). That withdrawal is taxed as ordinary income if the account has no after-tax basis.1


Every dollar you move to a Roth before then is a dollar that won’t count toward your future RMD calculations. The converted amount is taxable upfront, but Roth IRAs do not require RMDs during the owner’s lifetime.2 Once RMDs begin, you must take the required distribution before making a conversion, and that amount cannot be converted.


To calculate how much you can convert each year without moving into a higher tax bracket, subtract your taxable income before the conversion from the top of your current bracket. For[single filers in 2026](https://smartasset.com/taxes/current-federal-income-tax-brackets) , the 12% bracket ends at $50,400, the 22% bracket ends at $105,700 and the 24% bracket ends at $201,775.3 The table shows how the calculation works at different income levels:


Taxable Income Before Conversion Current Tax Bracket Top of Bracket Amount You Could Convert


$40,000 12% $50,400 $10,400 ($50,400 − $40,000)


$60,000 22% $105,700 $45,700 ($105,700 − $60,000)


$150,000 24% $201,775 $51,775 ($201,775 − $150,000)


The amount you convert adds to your taxable income and can increase both taxes and Medicare premiums. A higher tax rate applies only to income above the bracket threshold, while going over an IRMAA limit can increase your Medicare Part B and Part D premiums.


For 2026, surcharges begin above $109,000 for individual filers and $218,000 for joint filers.4 Medicare uses income from two years earlier, so a 2026 conversion could affect 2028 premiums. The IRMAA thresholds in effect for 2028 would determine whether a surcharge applies.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_retirement&utm_content=900kinirahereisyearlyrothconversionthatdodgesnexttaxbracket_a) can help you choose a conversion amount that fits your tax bracket and Medicare limits.**


## How Annual Roth Conversions Could Help You Save Almost $48,000


Let’s assume that you are 64, file individually and have $900,000 in an IRA with $60,000 in other[taxable income](https://smartasset.com/taxes/income-taxes) . You could[convert part of the IRA to a Roth each year](https://smartasset.com/retirement/convert-70k-annually-at-63-from-700k-in-ira-to-avoid-rmd) before RMDs begin at 75. This strategy would raise your taxes upfront, but reduce the balance that is used to calculate future RMDs.


To show how this works, the table breaks down an example using uses 2026 tax brackets. It does not include any[investment growth](https://smartasset.com/investing/investment-calculator) and compares how much you would pay in taxes during the[Roth conversion](https://smartasset.com/retirement/roth-conversion-taxes) years with what you would pay in your first RMD year:


Tax Event Total Taxable Income Taxes Paid


A year without a conversion $60,000 $7,912 ($1,240 at 10% on the first $12,400 + $4,560 at 12% on the next $38,000 + $2,112 at 22% on the next $9,600)


Each year of Roth conversions (64-74) $105,700 ($60,000 + $45,700 conversion) $17,966 ($1,240 at 10% on the first $12,400 + $4,560 at 12% on the next $38,000 + $12,166 at 22% on the next $55,300)


First RMD year at 75 with RMDs only $96,585 ($60,000 + $36,585 RMD) $15,961 ($1,240 at 10% on the first $12,400 + $4,560 at 12% on the next $38,000 + $10,161 at 22% on the next $46,185)


First RMD year at 75 after annual conversions $76,150 ($60,000 + $16,150 RMD) $11,465 ($1,240 at 10% on the first $12,400 + $4,560 at 12% on the next $38,000 + $5,665 at 22% on the next $25,750)


Over 11 years, you would move $502,700 into a Roth ($45,700 per year × 11) and leave $397,300 in the IRA ($900,000 − $502,700). Each conversion adds $10,054 to your tax bill ($17,966 − $7,912), which adds up to $110,594 ($10,054 × 11).


The conversions would also cut your first RMD from $36,585 to $16,150, lowering your federal tax by $4,496 in that first year alone. During the first 11 years of RMDs (between ages 75 and 85) annual Roth conversions would reduce your required withdrawals by $217,745 ($389,835 − $172,090). At a 22% tax rate, that would mean $47,904 less in federal taxes on those RMDs ($217,745 × 22%).


The $47,904 is the amount you would pay less in[taxes on future RMDs](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/how-to-avoid-taxes-on-rmd) , but it does not account for the $110,594 paid on the earlier conversions. Whether this strategy saves money overall depends on a number of variable factors, including your future income, tax rates and investment returns.
